newsitem.title: PERU: Superhero Metalman fails to end Peru hostage siege.
newsitem.headline: Superhero Metalman fails to end Peru hostage siege.

text.p: While hostages inside yearned to be free, a free market opened outside the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima as opportunists took advantage of the media spotlight to grab free publicity or sell their wares.

When a man dressed as a robot strode up to the besieged residence last weekend, children speculated that a superhero had arrived to end the three-week siege, but he was just promoting "Metalman," a comic book about to hit Lima newsstands.

The "Alpha and Omega" religious sect also took advantage of the international spotlight, distributing invitations to journalists to join them in meetings with beings from other planets. And local Indian medicine men, or shamans, were peddling their supernatural wares, offering public conjuring sessions to woo potential clients near the siege site.

Better-known commercial ventures have also seized on sales opportunities offered since Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movemement guerrillas stormed a reception at the Japanese ambassador's house on Dec. 17.

Telefonica del Peru has been distributing telephone cards since the first days of the crisis and has installed portable phones nearby. Pizza Hut has also been busy distributing leaflets advertising fast food to the crowds of journalists from around the world milling around the area.

Free Pepsi-Cola was being distributed, hawkers tried to sell step-ladders to photographers so they could get better shots of the booby-trapped house where the hostages were being held, and Peru's Channel Two television took its ratings battle to the site, distributing T-shirts and other promotional items.

While worried that the new outbreak of guerrilla violence will hit tourism, Lima travel agencies have determined to make the best of a bad situation and were offering tours as close to the hostage scene as security forces will allow.

But while a buzz of commerce surrounded them, the 20-odd heavily armed leftist rebels, who still held 74 hostages, were showing no signs of giving in and continued to press for the freedom of jailed comrades. Neither was President Alberto Fujimori, and many feared that a wrong move by either side could touch off the hairtrigger and cause a bloodbath.
